newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 10.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. For further information on these articles or details of BMC's other international press and broadcast services call Simon McMillan on "44 (0)171 256 5130 or e-mail bmc.co@ft.com
-- WHITEHALL MAY SHARE DATA IN BENEFIT FRAUD CRACKDOWN

Ministers are considering a crack down on housing benefit fraud, which costs an estimated 2bn stg per annum, by allowing a controversial flow of personal data from Whitehall to local authorities. The scheme would allow town halls to check personal details, such as change of address, by calling up a department of social security databases. It is however coming under fierce criticism from civil liberties groups.
-- EU PLANS LAWS ON PIRATE TV DECODERS

The European Commission is to outlaw the manufacture, promotion and sale of "pirate" decoders for pay-television and computer services under draft legislation proposed yesterday. The move could save the industry millions of Ecus. The industry estimates that up to five per cent of its turnover is lost through large scale piracy, however the current proposals still do not cover the individual pirates who copy work for personal or small scale use.
-- CEOS GET 'TWICE PAY OF OTHER DIRECTORS

Chief executives of the UKs largest companies are earning twice as much as any of their boardroom colleagues, according to a Monks Partnership Report. The report found that finance directors, the second most highly-paid directors, were on average earning more than half the pay of their chief executives and chairmen. Sales directors and research and development directors earned even less in comparison.
-- LORD SIMON SHARES ROW ESCALATES

The row over Lord Simon's retention of 2m stg of BP shares after becoming a minister escalated yesterday after it emerged that Lord Young sold all his holdings when he joined the government in 1979. Lord Young said it was the only way he had felt it would have possible to avoid conflict. John Redwood has called on Lord Simon to follow Lord Young's example "to protect himself and the government".
-- US CHART HIT BOOSTS MUSIC INDUSTRY

The Prodigy, the British music group have gone straight to the top of the American music chart, possibly signalling the opening of a substantial market for British music companies. Experimental music, as demonstrated by groups such as the Prodigy and the Chemical Brothers, has been hailed as the "next best thing" by the media at a time when the North American music scene has hit a creative hiatus.
-- CAPITAL RADIO CHIEF SET FOR TOP ITV JOB

Richard Eyre, group managing director of Capital Radio, is reputed to be about to accept the job of chief executive of the ITV Network Centre. If he does this may well signal the end of the declining fortunes of ITV. ITV has steadily been losing viewers to its rival the BBC for the last five years.
-- CALLS TO MOBILES 'STILL TOO HIGH'

Don Cruickshank of telecoms watchdog Oftel has warned British Telecommunications that the prices it is charging for calls to mobile phones are still too high, despite a third set of price cuts. BT announced on Wednesday daytime price cuts for calls to Vodafone and Cellnet from 37.5p per minute to 36.5p per minute, from 25p to 22p for evening calls and from 12.5p to 10.5p for weekend calls.
-- DRINKS GROUPS CONSIDER TIE-UP

Drinks giants Guinness and Grand Metropolitan are understood to have softened their opposition to a possible three-way link with LVMH, the French luxury goods firm which is opposing the 24bn stg mega-merger between the two UK groups. Any tie-up is likely to involve the combining of the wines and spirits businesses of Guinness and Grand Met with those of LVMH.
-- OUTCRY LEADS TO REPRIEVE FOR FIDS

The government is expected this week to announce an embarassing U-turn on plans announced in the Budget to end foreign income dividends (Fids). The move to allow companies with high levels of foreign income to continuing enjoying various tax benefits follows an outcry from some of Britain's biggest businesses and threat that some international companies could opt to relocate overseas.
-- McDONALDS TO RESTRUCTURE BUSINESS IN US

US fast food chain McDonald's has announced a dramatic restructuring of its US business in a bid to reinvigorate flagging domestic sales. Among the changes are the departure of Edward Rensi, the group's US chief executive, and the reorganisation of the business into five geographical divisions, each of which will operate independently.
